4.0.0.en: This shows us that the reason the Lord left the land of Judaea was the problems and comparisons that the Pharisees began to stir up between the baptism and followers of John on the one hand, and the baptism and disciples of Christ on the other (ch. 3).

4.0.1.en: Here the Lord Christ teaches us a spiritual lesson: that a person should avoid fruitless arguments, and even flee from them, lest he waste his time and effort and lose his peace to no benefit ...

4.0.2.en: "He must needs go through Samaria": this phrase carries two meanings. The first is simple: the geographical meaning, that Samaria lay on His way to Galilee. The deeper meaning is spiritual: that is, God "labored" for the salvation of the Samaritan woman, and for this reason He had to pass through Samaria so that He might meet her and speak with her.

4.0.3.en: How wonderful is Your plan, O Lord, for the salvation of my soul!

4.1.0.en: "Sychar": a town near Shechem, which is more famous, and in it was a well dug by Jacob to water his flocks and to affirm his ownership of these lands, since the well bore his name. Jacob had given this place to Joseph in preference to the rest of his brothers (see Gen 48:22), and this also confirms the descent of the Samaritans from their father Jacob.

4.1.1.en: "Wearied with His journey": all the interpreting Fathers of the Church paused over this verse in contemplation. Here is God who took our flesh and lived our life, and was wearied for our sake in order to offer us salvation ... He experienced pain and weariness as a man, so that we would have no excuse for not also being wearied in serving others. The distance He covered from His departure from Judaea to this town was 40 miles (the mile = 1,609.35 meters), that is, about 64 kilometers, bearing the hardship of walking in the heat for the salvation of one soul!

4.1.2.en: Among the wonderful parallels between what this story points to and the events of the Cross are what we see of thirst, weariness and the sixth hour, and the goal is salvation, whether for the Samaritan woman or for the whole world, and in both accounts the disciples left Him alone (v. 8).

4.1.3.en: So, is it a coincidence, or a clear prophetic sign, as a prelude to the events of the Cross? Nor should we overlook that the sixth hour here points to the condition of the Samaritan woman, for, because of her sin and bad reputation, she went out to draw water at a time when it was rare for other women to be present with her, so as to avoid their reproaches and their looks at her ... But Christ loves her and seeks her out!

4.2.s.en: (2) The meeting with the Samaritan woman

4.2.0.en: Since it was in God's prior arrangement and knowledge that He would meet the Samaritan woman, He sent all His disciples to buy food, so that He could meet the Samaritan woman alone. He thereby teaches us that, besides the ministry of teaching and preaching to the crowds, attention to individual work and the single soul is no less important than work with the masses, and also so that He would not shame her as she confessed her sins, as happens now in the sacrament of Confession. Christ asked the Samaritan woman for water to drink although He is "the fountain of living waters" (Jer 2:13, 17:13), and He is "the fountain of the water of life" (Rev 21:6), and He was sitting by the well as though in need of water; all this was so that He might enter her heart by humility.

4.2.1.en: Humility makes it easy for you to win the hearts of others and to convey the word of God to them.

4.2.2.en: The Samaritan woman's answer reminds us of the Lord's conversation with Nicodemus (ch. 3): man speaks of tangible material things, while Christ speaks of a deeper spiritual dimension ... What the Samaritan woman said was confined to the enmity existing between the Jews and the Samaritans, and her refusal was in a tone of disapproval so as to hide or forget her sin.

4.3.0.en: "If thou knewest the gift of God": Christ here addresses the Samaritan woman and every soul; it is He who wills, and He begins the conversation with her in dialogue.

4.3.1.en: And we, sadly, do not realize the dimensions of this great gift, otherwise this would not be our state. We are still seeking the water of the world and its material things and its desires, although we know that there is no satisfaction or quenching from it, forgetting the source of true riches that fills every material, psychological and spiritual thirst and need; He is the true God who wants to give you everything ... And whoever accepts God's gift rises above the whole world and will never thirst. God's gift does not make a person content with it only, but he becomes a spring that waters the needs of others, like a channel that carries the current of a great river, so that it is first watered itself, and every thirsty person draws from it ... And this is the source of the spiritual richness of man which we have seen in all the saints, the early ones and the contemporary ... And the most wonderful thing is that this divine current that God gives, which is the indwelling of the Holy Spirit in man, never leaves him, even to eternal life.

4.3.2.en: As for the Samaritan woman, she still does not grasp the Lord's speech; at one time she wonders where He gets this water when He has nothing to draw with (v. 11), and at another she wants this water in its material form, so that she would not have to come back to this well bearing the hardship of the road. Her state even reached the point of mocking Him, for of course He is not better than Jacob and his sons who drank from it, so how could He get better water than this well?!

4.4.0.en: In this she brings us back again to what we began with, which is the nature of the human being who does not realize God's gift of the indwelling and outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

4.5.s.en: (3) Christ reveals Himself to the Samaritan woman

4.5.0.en: After the Lord Christ spoke of spiritual things in a hidden manner in which He prepared her to ask for the living water, He revealed Himself directly, but only to the extent she could bear. He asked her to bring her husband if she truly desired this living water, and the woman answered with half the truth, that she had no lawful husband, thereby hiding her sin of living with a man without marriage. But the surprise with which Christ astounded her, in declaring that He knew all her past, and even the present she was living, shook her conscience, and so her reply came, which represents the first spark of her faith, as she said, "Sir," after she had at first refused to speak with Him because He was a Jew; then she also testified that He is "a prophet," after she had been mocking and saying, "Art thou greater than our father Jacob?" Dear one ... in the previous conversation we see a glimpse which we may learn from the person of our beloved God, namely His wonderful gentleness in breaking into this sinful soul. He knows her state and her sin, yet look at Him as He praises her twice, once before He declares His knowledge of her sin, and once again after He has declared this knowledge, beginning His speech with the phrase "Thou hast well said," and ending His speech with the phrase "in that saidst thou truly." And with this gentleness, He did not neglect to declare the truth so that this woman might repent of her sin ... Would that we all might learn this manner: God did not smear her over, though He is the Judge, but He exposed the error for the sake of her repentance and not her destruction.

4.5.1.en: Do we treat sinners with this gentleness, with the difference that we are sinners and under judgment? Let us take this exercise for our lives: to praise the faint ray of light in every person before directing him.

4.6.0.en: When the Samaritan woman realized that the Lord was not an ordinary person but a prophet, her speech turned to another direction, as she was occupied with the religious dispute between the Jews and the Samaritans, and each side's claim to the correctness of its faith, and it was as if, after realizing His distinguished person, she forgot the story of the water and the well and became concerned with the salvation of her soul. And when the Lord saw that the woman had become prepared, He began to speak to her about true worship and its concept, which is not tied to place but to manner, for God does not accept the worship of the body without the spirit.

4.6.1.en: "In spirit and in truth they must worship": it means worship with contrition and the sense of God's presence. As for bodily and merely numerical worship, God does not accept it, but man is deceived by it in his spiritual practices. And despite this spiritual disclosure about worshiping God in every place, the Lord did not neglect to make clear that the Jewish faith in its essence is the sound faith and not the faith of the Samaritans, and that the awaited salvation has its source in the Jews (v. 22).

4.6.2.en: "The hour cometh, and now is": a clear indication of the appearance of the awaited Messiah, the end of both the Jewish and the Samaritan worship, and the transition to true spiritual worship.

4.6.3.en: It is also noted that the Lord Christ corrected the form and manner of worship without abolishing it, for prostration is a duty owed to God; it is an offering of love, respect, contrition, and a feeling of the heart that reflects man's sense of being in the true presence of God. The Church teaches her children prostration, whether in public worship such as the Divine Liturgy, or at the personal and individual level of man in his daily prayers.

4.7.0.en: The woman continued her spiritual conversation, and referred to the coming Christ who knows all things. And when she reached this stage in which she carried her hope of awaiting the Savior, the hope of the Jews and the Samaritans, Christ answered her, declaring Himself and revealing Himself: "I ... am He." The person of Christ is the only One who can dissolve differences, disputes and enmity, and in Him all become one ... For many problems and disagreements, especially marital ones, find no solution because both parties insist on keeping Christ away from their lives. But if He enters, there will be neither Samaria nor Judaea, but humility, contrition, a sense of the Lord's presence, and obedience to His commandment ... Would that You, beloved Lord, were inside every home.

4.8.0.en: Why did the disciples marvel? Because Jewish teaching forbade a man to speak with a woman in a public place, even if she were his wife, and they did not understand Christ's concern for preaching and salvation. "No man said": a clear indication of the disciples' respect for their Teacher, and it is one of the Christian manners that the Lord mentioned: "The disciple is not above his master" (Mt 10:24); "The disciple is not above his master: but every one that is perfect shall be as his master" (Lk 6:40).

4.8.1.en: And this spirit our Church received in what is called the life of discipleship ... and it requires true humility of heart before the Church's teachers, priests and servants ...

4.9.0.en: The Samaritan woman believed, and expressed her faith positively by setting out to her village to preach it, and the word "Is not" here does not carry doubt in her faith, but an incentive to the people to go out and make sure for themselves. "The woman then left her waterpot": it has a beautiful spiritual meaning, which is that the soul that loves Christ cannot but tell others about Him, even if it leaves its various concerns that hinder its progress from serving God, such as the love of money and position ...

4.10.0.en: A dialogue about food, in which the disciples took the earlier position of the Samaritan woman, for the Lord Christ speaks of spiritual food, "ye know not of," while they thought that someone had brought Him something to eat ... And this does not mean that Christ did not need food, being a perfect man like us, but it is a difference in priorities, for hunger and thirst for the salvation of the human soul have the priority.

4.11.0.en: Despite the exhaustion after the long journey, and His bodily need for water and food, the Lord Christ considered doing the will of His Father in calling man to salvation, and completing His work of redemption on the wood of the Cross, to be His true food, and indeed the desire of His heart, offering a new proof of His love and longing for the salvation of the human soul.

4.11.1.en: Then Christ moved to a real scene when He said: "Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields" ... Although the season of harvest was four months away, there was a harvest of another kind, for all the people of Samaria came out from the village of Sychar in their white garments in great groups after the woman's good news, and the fields were filled with them, and the Lord Christ regarded them as a spiritual harvest ready to be reaped with the sickle of faith.

4.12.0.en: God is not unrighteous to forget a man's labor, so everyone who gathers souls for the Kingdom of God receives an earthly and heavenly reward with joy, and partnership with all who went before him. And Christ, in His faithfulness, remembers the labor of everyone who went before in preparing this seed for harvest, although He is the true Sower who causes His word to grow. Here He points to the prophets of the Old Testament in their labor and their preparing of the people for four thousand years, and this is also a lesson for the disciples, preserving their humility, that whatever fruit they will reap in preaching is the result of the labor of others. And the truth is that in the field of service, the sower cannot be separated from the reaper, for whoever reaps now from the labor of him who sowed before is also sowing for another reaper after him, and this is what the Lord meant in (v. 37) using one of the well-known Jewish proverbs, that it is not necessary for the servant to see the fruits of his service; for Christ Himself, despite the perfection of His labor and redemption, the fruits of Christianity came after His ascension to heaven.

4.12.1.en: Beloved ... does this not tempt you to share in these joys ... the joys of the labor of service ... the joys of the harvest ... the joys of calling others to the Kingdom of God, so that you may be a sower and a reaper with a heavenly wage? Blessed are you if you do so.

4.13.s.en: (7) The beginning of Christ's ministry in Galilee

4.13.0.en: In continuing the journey to Galilee, after stopping in Samaria, the Lord did not stay in Nazareth, the place of His first upbringing, which did not believe in Him and did not accept His preaching. And because this action of the Lord might raise questions, St. John indicated the reason for Christ's not entering it by His own words about it: "that a prophet hath no honor in his own country." As for the Galileans, they accepted Christ and welcomed Him, for they had seen Him during their visit to Jerusalem at the time of the feast, and they passed on reports about Him ...

4.14.0.en: "A certain nobleman" [lit. servant of the king]: the king here is Herod Antipas, who was the ruler responsible for this region (Galilee), and the Jews called him king. The distance this servant covered from Capernaum to Galilee was about 25 kilometers, and this shows the intensity of his attachment to the healing of his son and his knocking on every possible door ... As for the Lord Christ's answer (v. 48), it deserves our thought and contemplation, for He directs our minds to the true faith that does not require miracles to prove it, since it is firm and deeper than the working of miracles or wonders, and does not need material evidence to demonstrate it.

4.15.0.en: And yet Christ did not disappoint the man's hope, for He is the One who said: "him that cometh to Me I will in no wise cast out" (ch. 6:37), so His answer carried all the divine authority in healing, and even in raising from the dead, and the man believed in the power of Christ's word, and did not insist on taking Him with him to Capernaum.

4.16.0.en: Here the completion of the miracle is announced, and it is highlighted that the hour of the son's healing corresponded to the hour of the man's conversation with Christ.

4.16.1.en: "The second miracle": an indication that the first sign was at the wedding in Cana of Galilee.

4.16.2.en: Perhaps, dear reader, we find that faith is the pivot of the preceding miracle, for the man's faith and hope were what first drove him to walk 25 kilometers to meet Christ, and to ask the Lord to heal his son, confident in His power to do so, and so he obtained the healing of his boy.

4.16.3.en: Chapter five: the sick man of Bethesda; the authority of Christ
